html:
Projective Invariance

The cross-ratio isolates a fundamental geometric property of four points that is preserved perfectly across perspective projections.

INTERACTIVE ELEMENTS:

  • Drag center O to change the perspective rays.
  • Drag points P₁, P₂, P₃, P₄ along their line to adjust the core cross-ratio.
  • Drag any magenta line to translate the transversals and observe the invariant mapping.
⚠ Figure failed to load

plan.contextChunk: This figure illustrates the cross-ratio, a projective invariant used in single-view 3D scene understanding. It shows sets of collinear points P, Q, and R related by the cross-ratio, projected from a center of projection O. The point R1 lies at infinity because the line connecting the R points is parallel to the line passing through O, P1, and Q1. The figure demonstrates how if two sets of points, related by a projection, have the same ordering, then their cross ratio will be preserved.

interactionPlan.concept: The cross-ratio of four collinear points is a projective invariant that remains constant regardless of the center of projection or the orientation of the transversal line.
elements: Center of projection O (black dot with label)
Four black projection rays extending rightward from O
Magenta transversal line P, closest to O
Magenta transversal line Q, in the middle
Magenta transversal line R, furthest right and strictly parallel to the bottom-most ray
Intersection points P1, P2, P3, P4 on line P (black dots with subscript labels)
Intersection points Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 on line Q (black dots with subscript labels)
Intersection points R2, R3, R4 on line R (black dots with subscript labels)
Label 'R1 → ∞' associated with line R

interactions.teaches: Moving the projection center O changes the angles of the rays and the intersection locations on the transversals, while preserving the fundamental projective invariants.
Translating or rotating the transversals alters individual intersection distances, demonstrating that the cross-ratio remains constant for any line cutting the pencil of rays.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The cross-ratio isolates a fundamental geometric property of four points that cannot be destroyed by perspective projection.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Initialize the figure showing all elements (P, Q, and R, along with O and the rays) simultaneously so it serves as a complete static drop-in. Place O on the far left. Draw 4 black rays expanding to the right. Draw 3 magenta transversal lines intersecting them. Line R MUST be drawn strictly parallel to the bottom ray, so it only intersects the top three rays. For subscript point labels, strictly use correct SVG.js v3 nested text syntax (e.g., layerLabels.text(add => { add.tspan(str); if(sub) add.tspan(sub).dy(5); })) so both the base letter and subscript render correctly. Do NOT draw any floating cross-ratio math calculation boxes; keep the visual composition identical to the clean geometric source image.

demo_steps.title: Defining the Cross-Ratio
demo_steps.narration: Four collinear points P1–P4 define a cross-ratio based on their relative distances. Drag the points along the line to change this fundamental value.

demo_steps.title: Central Projection
demo_steps.narration: Projecting these points from center O to a new line Q creates points Q1–Q4. Try moving O — the distances change drastically, but the cross-ratio is preserved.

demo_steps.title: Points at Infinity
demo_steps.narration: If a transversal line R is parallel to one of the rays, its intersection R1 lies at infinity. The cross-ratio still holds, with the infinite terms taking a limit of 1.

plan.keyInsight: The cross-ratio isolates a fundamental geometric property of four points that cannot be destroyed by perspective projection, making it a powerful tool for recognizing 3D structures from 2D images.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Place point O on the far left. Draw 4 black rays expanding to the right. Draw 3 magenta transversal lines intersecting them. Line P is steepest, Q is less steep, and R is shallow. Line R MUST be drawn strictly parallel to the bottom ray (Ray 1), so it never intersects it, only intersecting Rays 2, 3, and 4 at R2, R3, R4. Place black dots at all intersections. Add an on-screen math display showing CR(P) = CR(Q) = CR(R) = [value], updating dynamically.

discrepancies: The Q and R transversal lines cross each other between Ray 3 and Ray 4 in the source figure, placing R₄ between P₄ and Q₄ on the top ray. In the generated figure, they do not cross, leaving Q₄ as the middle point.
The 'R₁ → ∞' label is clipped by the right edge of the viewport, obscuring the infinity symbol.
The labels for P₁-P₄ are positioned to the right of their respective points, causing visual clutter with the interior rays, whereas the source places them cleanly to the left.
The transversal lines (particularly Q) have noticeably different slopes compared to the source figure, altering the overall geometric proportions.
evaluation.notes: The figure accurately models the projective geometry and includes excellent drag interactions, but the specific slopes of the transversals fail to capture the crossing of Q and R present in the source, and some labels suffer from poor placement or clipping.
action_items: Adjust the initial coordinates of the Q line (QA, QB) so that it crosses the R line between Ray 3 and Ray 4, matching the source intersection order (P₄, R₄, Q₄) on the top ray.
Shift the P₁-P₄ labels to the left of their points (e.g., subtract from x instead of adding) to match the source and reduce interior clutter.
Adjust the R line's maximum extension or move the rightmost label slightly left to ensure 'R₁ → ∞' is fully visible without clipping at the SVG boundary.
Consider adding a live text readout of the calculated cross-ratio value for each line to explicitly verify the 'projective invariance' concept for the user.
